Seeing that it has been pretty well occupied for come time past in killing its own measures, or in permitting them to be knocked on the head by its par- liamentary critics, it ;gust be admitted that 1 the process of political' sepulture must be so I familiar to the Government undertakers as 1 1 to qualify them for the successful disposal of any questions of a funereal character. I That they are rapidly preparing the country I for the celebration of their own obsequitn, all those whe have impartially watched the conduct of the Government on almost every question of national interest and importance will only be denied by those of its supporters in the country or the press, who are always I ready with the cry 'The King is dead ; long I live the King." We do not forget, when I speaking of the Government as laudably dig. ' ging its own grave, that its supporters , still point to its parliamentary majority. ' Parliamentary majorities, we know, are not to be unduly disparaged, even when they are only "mechanical majorities," but any- body acquainted with the history and vi- cissitudes of parliamentary majorities ' "mechanical," or otherwise, are aware that! Government majorities, are like other kinds of riches, and are liable to take unto them- 1 selves wings. We are assured on familiar authority that "Wine is a good familiar creature, when well used." The same may be said of the majorities which are found at the heels of a Government which is always dexterously continuing to escape the "me- chanical" defeat of a parliamentary division, by turning its back upon itself and accep- ting defeat without it. Lord Beaconalield's contempt for the "Coffee-house babble" which authenticated Turkish slaughter and wrung the heart of England, gave place at lest to confessions of error and to a little of that sobbing rhetoric which costa so little to a veteran and accomplished actor, Even the Premier will now admit that the Turk is somewhat reprehensible on the 1 score of taste and that, to say the I least of it, his massacres have been ill-advised and politically inexpedient, not to say embarrassing to his political suppor- ters in the British Government. But Turks will be Turks you know and—its their way. I Perhaps when that general election comes, which certainly looms in the not distant I future, the oonstituenoies—which at Oldham and elsewhere, have already spoken omin- ously at the Poll—may have some words of mild reproof for a Government, which has been the persevering apologist of some of the most unspeakable butcheries which have ever darkened the annals of semi-civilised or barbarous races. The intrinsic value of the Government majorities were strangely 'hewn a few days since, when it acquiesced, at the moment, in Mr. Clare Read'. Bill, al- ' though ;t.'.' whips had moved heaven and ...th to crow, th,; !ions° with. its mechani- cal majority. And so the man who had left a Government which had shown itself unwill- ing or powerless to fulfill its own pledgee to its own supporter., brought this omnipotent Goveznment to its knees and taught it how little respect the country has for Cabi- nets, which forget their obligations and the constituencies to which, after all, they owe their existence. The defeat of the Government during the present week, in the matter of the Stock Exchange, when Sir Stafford Northcote, after labouring to prove the futility of the proposal, suddenly turned round and consented to swallow it, would be i ludicrous indeed, were not the spectacle so humiliating. No Government can long ' survive the public scorn inspired by such 1 flagrant political incompetence, and which, in the matter of a policy, betrays a condition of such incredible mendicity. The Government Burials Bill already threatens to be of the same tentative and I spiritless character. The unconsecrated ground is not to be provided because any persons, so far as we know, object to bury their dead relations in consecrated soil ; but [only be- cause by the existing law consecration in- volves the exclusive use of the service of the Church of England. To change the legal I force of consecration so as to allow of the performance in consecrated ground of the 1 re'erions services of persons of all creeds ' would rem,eri the difficulty, and it would I probably be fount; that in seven or eight villages out of every ten thie .."resent,church- yard would be adequate for all the of the the parish for generations to come.'
